title: RCMP kill gunman
subtitle: VLT losses may have led to man's rage: [Final Edition] - ProQuest
article: According to the RCMP, 38-year-old Shawn Martinot was killed around 2:30 a.m. Monday when he emerged from his room with a gun. He had been flushed out with tear gas, delivered by an RCMP robot sent into his room.

There are reports Martinot, an itinerant labourer who lives from paycheque-to-paycheque, became enraged when he lost his money on VLT machines. He allegedly returned from his room with his rifle and shot up the machine, according to some residents in the northern town of about 2,600 on the shores of Lac La Ronge.
The incident began around 10:30 a.m. Sunday when Martinot walked into the lounge of the hotel carrying a rifle. He was disarmed by an employee and police were called.
Before the La Ronge RCMP arrived Martinot had returned to his room where it was believed he had more weapons.
Shots were heard from the hotel room on two or three occasions, which confirmed there were more guns, but RCMP won't say how many were found in the room.

The hotel and part of a neighbouring apartment building were evacuated. The RCMP emergency response team, based in Regina, flew into La Ronge and tried to negotiate with Martinot for several hours but failed to convince him to give himself up.
After the tear gas was released, Martinot fired at the robot, disabling it. He came out of his room and walked down the hallway towards officers, still carrying the gun, said Russell.
He was shot and killed when he refused to put the gun down and continued walking towards the officers, she said.

"The RCMP and all officers are trained to end the threat. They shoot to end the behaviour of the threat that is occurring," said Russell, noting such situations "are very difficult" on any police officer.
Fortunately, no one other than Martinot was injured. Counseling will be offered to the officers involved and they will be encouraged to take time off but it is not mandatory, said Russell.

An internal review of the incident will be conducted by the RCMP, which is standard procedure whenever an officer discharges a weapon. Russell couldn't comment on whether Martinot's weapon was pointed at any officers, saying that will be part of the review.
"All those details will have to be determined," she said.
The RCMP major crimes unit and forensic identification officers were at the scene Monday.
"He seemed like a half-decent guy," Harris said, noting Martinot was taking medication for a mental illness and went off of it recently.
"And he was drinking pretty heavy Saturday night" at the Northland Hotel bar, Harris added.
The RCMP won't talk about Martinot's medical history, said Russell.
"It's premature to try and speculate on what might have been motivation or cause for the behaviour -- what might have sparked this incident. It's too soon to say," she said.

According to Harris, Martinot moved to town about two years ago from Flin Flon, Manitoba. He relocated on the recommendation of a friend who worked at the La Ronge Motor Hotel and Outdoor Adventure Company two blocks away on the same street as the Northland.
No one at the La Ronge Motor Hotel would talk to the media Monday.
"We've got a standard policy here and we do not want anyone querying anybody at this hotel about what happened," said the manager, who abruptly hung up the phone.
The owner of the Northland Hotel also owns Northland Taxi, for which Martinot did maintenance work.

Bill Hawke, a retiree who helps out at the La Ronge Motor Hotel, told The StarPhoenix on Sunday evening that staff from the Northland were evacuated by the RCMP and gathered at his establishment to have coffee.
"I think he might have done something to get attention but it got out of hand," Hawke said Sunday, adding, "But I think he'll be okay. He'll come to his senses."
Harris also assumed Martinot would give up before things reached a crisis.
"It surprised me that he didn't come out, especially when they used tear gas on him. But then he came out and shot their robot, disabled it, and that's when they opened up on him," Harris said.
"I think if they would have let someone in there who really knew him, to talk to him, they might have been able to talk him out. But they wouldn't let anyone in there because he had a rifle."

Resident Cindy Nicholson, who watched the drama through her apartment window, said police cruisers, with their lights flashing, screeched to a halt in front of the Northland and officers drew their weapons. Parishioners at a nearby church were detained by the police for some time after the morning service until it was determined to be safe to leave, she said.
